facts.text: Earth's magnetic field flipped from normal polarity (the Gauss Chron) to reversed polarity (the Matuyama Chron) about 2.58 Ma.
The reversal marks the base of the Gelasian and so the start of the Pleistocene and the Quaternary; the boundary stratotype is at Monte San Nicola, Sicily.
It coincides with a minor extinction of calcareous nannofossils, including Discoaster pentaradiatus and Discoaster surculus.
The weakened field may have left Earth's surface unshielded for about 15,000 years from the radiation of an early Pleistocene supernova.
In 2009 the boundary was moved down to 2.58 Ma to match key changes in Earth's climate, oceans and life at that time.

conflicts.note: Pleistocene page, quoting the 2009 IUGS decision

facts.text: Around 2.58 Ma ice sheets began to spread across the Northern Hemisphere, starting the Quaternary glaciation, which is still going on.
The Quaternary's start is tied to the formation of the Arctic ice cap; Greenland had been icing over since the late Pliocene.
Glacials and interglacials then alternated, with mean temperatures falling and the swings between them growing through the Pleistocene.
At the height of glacials, ice sheets at least 4 km thick covered parts of Europe, North America and Siberia.
In the first Pleistocene glacial, Patagonian ice reached the present Argentine coast.

title: Mastodons and gomphotheres vanish outside the Americas

facts.text: During the Early Pleistocene all non-elephantid proboscideans outside the Americas died out, including mammutids, gomphotheres and deinotheres; only Stegodon survived.

events.date_text: during the Early Pleistocene, 2.60–0.77 million years ago (2.58–0.774 Ma)

title: Eltanin asteroid impact in the South Pacific

facts.text: An asteroid about 1–4 km wide hit the deep ocean at the edge of the Bellingshausen Sea, about 1,500 km southwest of Chile.
It struck sea floor 4–5 km deep and left no known crater; the site was found from an iridium anomaly in sediment cores.
The impact probably vaporised about 150 km³ of water and raised tsunami waves hundreds of metres high.

verification.title: The Eltanin asteroid impact: possible South Pacific palaeomegatsunami footprint and potential implications for the Pliocene–Pleistocene transition

title: Aridification at the start of the Pleistocene

facts.text: Bipolar glaciation dried the globe, speeding a long decline in the functional diversity of hoofed mammals around 2.5 Ma.
In Africa a cooling and drying trend about 2.5 Ma coincided with the rise of thick-molared Homo rudolfensis and Paranthropus.
In Australia an aridification event at 2.56 Ma may be linked to the onset of continental glaciation in the Arctic.
Around 2.5 Ma the Omo–Turkana Basin mixed forest, woodland, grassland and bushland, with grasslands spreading through the Early Pleistocene.

verification.title: Two major ecological shifts shaped 60 million years of ungulate faunal evolution

title: Early Homo and robust australopithecines radiate

facts.text: About 2.5 Ma hominin fossils in East Africa become extraordinarily diverse, with robust australopithecines and early Homo appearing first in the Turkana Basin.
This apparent adaptive radiation of hominins straddles the Pliocene–Pleistocene boundary.
The first Homo species appeared about 2.5 Ma; earlier hominins had kept their tree-climbing habits until then.
Brain size rose quickly, and by 2 Ma the first animals classed in the genus Homo had appeared.
Paranthropus and early Homo coexisted at the start of the Pleistocene, but only Homo erectus remained for much of it.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth: emergence of the genus Homo at the start of the Pleistocene
History of Earth: first Homo had appeared by 2 Ma

facts.text: About 2.5 Ma waters from Ethiopia flowed north for the first time and joined the ancestral Egyptian Nile.
Uplift of the Rwenzori Mountains turned paleolake Obweruka's drainage east and began forming Lake Victoria, which did not yet drain north.
The earliest species of the sabre-toothed cat Smilodon and the short-faced bear Arctodus evolved about 2.5 Ma.
The earliest species, S. gracilis, lived from 2.5 million to 500,000 years ago and probably evolved from Megantereon; it reached northern South America in the Great American Interchange.
Smilodon lived in the Americas until at latest 8,200 years ago and was perhaps the last of the sabre-toothed cats.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth lists Smilodon under c. 2.58 Ma

facts.text: Paranthropus boisei, a robust australopithecine, lived in East Africa about 2.5 to 1.15 million years ago; its oldest remains, from Malema, are about 2.3 million years old.
It is found at Koobi Fora and in Olduvai Gorge Beds I and II, persisting after H. habilis gave way to H. erectus around 1.6 Ma.
The 1.7-million-year-old skull KNM-ER 406, with a 510 cc brain, shows several hominin species shared Africa at once.

verification.title: Hominin Taxic Diversity
verification.note: The 4.5 Ma date is for the earliest claimed hominin taxic diversity, not Paranthropus boisei's range.

title: Lake Bungunnia dams the Murray River

facts.text: Earth movements blocked the Murray River near Swan Reach, creating vast freshwater Lake Bungunnia, which lasted from 2.5 to 0.5 Ma.
The damming followed more than 250 m of uplift in the Grampians of Victoria about 2.5 Ma.

title: Pre-Illinoian glaciations reach Kansas and Missouri

facts.text: North America went through repeated Pre-Illinoian glacial and interglacial periods from about 2.5 to 0.2 million years ago.
Researchers found 11 distinct glaciations in this span, not the two once assumed, and discarded the old Nebraskan, Aftonian, Kansan and Yarmouthian stages.
The Laurentide Ice Sheet reached as far south as the Missouri and Ohio river valleys, and to Douglas County, Kansas.
Later Illinoian ice sheets pushed farther south still, to near Carbondale, Illinois.
Patchy Pre-Illinoian glacial drift more than 500,000 years old survives in parts of the Driftless Area of the upper Mississippi.

End of the stage correlated with the end of MIS 9
End of the stage correlated with the start of MIS 6 (OSL dating in Illinois)

title: Last seaway link across Panama closes

facts.text: The last shallow, temporary sea connection through the Central American Seaway ended no later than 2.45 Ma.
Deep-ocean connections had already closed between 12 and 9.2 Ma, after a collision that began about 25 Ma.
Surface-water exchange that kept Atlantic and Pacific salinities alike ended about 4.6 Ma; a last definite temporary breach came as recently as 2.45 Ma.

conflicts.note: genetic-drift data hint that surface ocean connections may have lasted until about 1 Ma

title: Amazon River takes its present shape

facts.text: The Amazon, a transcontinental river since 11.8–11.3 Ma, took its present shape about 2.4 million years ago.

title: Loess begins piling up on China's Loess Plateau

facts.text: Crustal movement and a cold climate started loess deposition on the Loess Plateau about 2.4 Ma.
Tibetan uplift had set up the East Asian monsoon, and the drier Quaternary climate weathered out the silt that became loess.

title: Sundaland emerges and mammals reach Java

facts.text: Sundaland emerged around 2.4 Ma; before then Java had no mammals.
As sea level fell, animals such as the dwarf elephant relative Sinomastodon bumiajuensis colonised Sundaland from mainland Asia.
Oldowan stone tools flourished in eastern Africa and spread to southern Africa between 2.4 and 1.7 million years ago.
Securely dated Oldowan artefacts 2.4–1.9 million years old at Ain Boucherit, Algeria, carry the industry into North Africa.
At Swartkrans, South Africa, Oldowan tools of 2.2–1.8 Ma lie with Paranthropus robustus fossils; a polished bone point there dates to 1.8–1.5 Ma.
Oldowan toolmakers also left Africa: by 1.8 Ma early Homo with Oldowan tools lived at Dmanisi, Georgia.
Acheulean tools appeared about 1.7 Ma, yet Oldowan assemblages went on being made beside them; other traditions supplanted the Oldowan only by about 0.25 Ma.

conflicts.date_text: until at least 1.7 million years ago
conflicts.note: Oldowan lead: end of the main Oldowan period (minimum)

title: Homo habilis lives in East and South Africa

facts.text: Homo habilis, the 'handy man', lived in East and South Africa from about 2.4 to 1.65 million years ago.
Its brain ranged from about 500 to 900 cm³, and it may still have climbed trees like the australopithecines.
It made Oldowan stone tools and, unlike australopithecines, ate much meat, probably scavenged.
Around 2 Ma it may have built the first structures, stones propping up branches; a 1.75 Ma stone circle at Olduvai is the oldest claimed architecture.
Whether it was the direct ancestor of Homo erectus is now debated.

title: Giant ground sloths reach North America

facts.text: Eremotherium eomigrans, the first megatheriid ground sloth in North America, arrived 2.2 Ma across the new Panamanian land bridge.
Going the other way, horses that entered South America in the Great American Interchange evolved into Hippidion around 2.5 Ma.
Possible stone artefacts at Shangchen, central China, are dated by magnetostratigraphy to 2.12 Ma, about 300,000 years before Dmanisi.
If confirmed, they are the oldest known stone tools outside Africa.
Pebble tools are also reported from Yiron, Israel, at 2.4 Ma, Riwat, Pakistan, at 2.0 Ma and Renzidong, China, at over 2 Ma.
They suggest Homo habilis or an ancestral species may have spread across Asia.
Tools perhaps 2.48 million years old from the Zarqa Valley, Jordan, could likewise mean a hominin earlier than H. erectus left Africa.

sources.title: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

verification.title: Hominin occupation of the Chinese Loess Plateau since about 2.1 million years ago

facts.text: A single huge eruption in the Tauranga Volcanic Centre produced the Waiteariki ignimbrite, about 870 ± 87 km³ of dense rock.
The supereruption probably came from the Omanawa Caldera, known only from a gravity anomaly.
At least eight other large eruptions struck the Tauranga Volcanic Centre between 2.4 and 1.9 million years ago.

facts.text: Yellowstone volcanism began 2.15 Ma; its first and largest cycle climaxed in the eruption of the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff.
The VEI 8 eruption produced about 2,450–2,500 km³ of material and left the Island Park Caldera, roughly 80 by 65 km.
It made about 2,500 times as much ash as Mount St. Helens in 1980; the ash is found from southern California to St. Louis.
Part of the tuff records the Huckleberry Ridge geomagnetic excursion and is dated very precisely to 2.0773 ± 0.0034 Ma.
The oldest identified Homo erectus is DNH 134, a 2.04-million-year-old skull from Drimolen, South Africa, which lived alongside Paranthropus robustus.
Other early fossils include the roughly 1.9-million-year-old KNM-ER 2598 and the cranium KNM-ER 3733 from Koobi Fora, Kenya.
Its populations spread through grassland and woodland savannas, which were expanding with global aridification at the onset of the Quaternary glaciation.
H. ergaster, often treated as African H. erectus, was the first human with a slender, modern body plan.
Most H. erectus fossils date from 1.8 to 1 Ma; the species lasted until about 0.6 Ma and was long the only hominin.

sources.title: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

verification.title: Contemporaneity of Australopithecus , Paranthropus , and early Homo erectus in South Africa

facts.text: Large ignimbrite eruptions continued in the central Andes, including the 550 km³ Galán ignimbrite about 2.1 Ma.
After 2 Ma activity in the Altiplano–Puna volcanic complex waned; after 1 Ma it was mostly andesitic, with no large ignimbrites.

title: Homo first spreads out of Africa
article: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

facts.text: The earliest hominins outside Africa date to close to 2 million years ago, at the start of expansions led by Homo erectus.
In the Early Pleistocene archaic Homo arose in Africa and spread throughout Afro-Eurasia, in waves known together as Out of Africa I.
Key early sites are Riwat in Pakistan (about 2 Ma), Dmanisi in the Caucasus (1.81 Ma) and Ubeidiya in the Levant (1.5 Ma).
Favourable climate swings probably opened the Levantine corridor to the adaptable Homo erectus, perhaps only at times.
The dispersal has been linked to the Saharan pump around 1.9 Ma; by 2.0–1.5 Ma hominins were settling southern Europe and Asia.

sources.title: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

facts.text: Homo rudolfensis lived in East Africa about 2 million years ago; most of its fossils come from Koobi Fora and date to 1.9–1.85 Ma.
Fossils from Ethiopia and Malawi dated 2.5–2.4 Ma could make it the earliest known Homo, but which specimens belong to it is disputed.
Its molar enamel was almost as thick as that of Paranthropus.

conflicts.note: Shungura and Uraha remains, if H. rudolfensis

title: Kap København ecosystem preserved in ancient DNA

facts.text: Environmental DNA from the Kap København Formation in northern Greenland is at least two million years old, from the Early Pleistocene.
It records mastodons, Arctic hares, geese, poplar, birch and willow trees, horseshoe crabs and corals; mastodons evidently ranged much farther north than once thought.
The site's average minimum temperature is reconstructed at more than 10 °C warmer than today.
The sabre-toothed thylacosmilids, among South America's only large mammalian carnivores in the Pliocene, died out about 2 Ma.
Placental counterparts such as dogs, weasels and sabre-toothed cats entered South America only in the early Pleistocene.
The terror bird Titanis, which had crossed into North America, died out there about 1.8 Ma, perhaps outcompeted by carnivorans.
Bears, cats and skunks reached South America by about 1 Ma, when the short-faced bear Arctotherium first appears there.

title: Taupō Rift and Volcanic Zone form

facts.text: The Taupō Rift and the old Taupō Volcanic Zone formed in New Zealand about 2 Ma, ending major activity in the Coromandel Volcanic Zone.
The postulated Omanawa Caldera sat where the old and new rifts met around 2 Ma.

title: Congo River basin takes its present shape

facts.text: Between about 2.0 and 1.5 Ma the basin of the Congo River acquired its present shape.

title: Colorado River deepens the Grand Canyon
article: Geology of the Grand Canyon area

facts.text: Wetter ice-age climates from about 2 Ma swelled the Colorado River, which cut the Grand Canyon faster than ever before.
The canyon had almost reached its modern depth by 1.2 million years ago.
Nearby, the upper half of Zion Canyon was carved between about 2 and 1 million years ago.

sources.title: Geology of the Grand Canyon area
Geology of the Zion and Kolob canyons area

facts.text: Australopithecus sediba is known from two partial skeletons, a juvenile and an adult female, in Malapa Cave, South Africa, about 1.98 million years old.
It lived alongside Paranthropus robustus and Homo ergaster/erectus; Malapa may have been a natural death trap.
Once proposed as an ancestor of Homo, it may instead be a late-surviving relative of A. africanus; the question is contested.
Acheulean technology, derived from the Oldowan, first developed about 2 million years ago; finds from Ethiopia date to 1.95 Ma.
Homo erectus is credited with inventing it by 1.95 Ma, inheriting Oldowan technology and refining it.
Early Acheulean tools from West Turkana, Kenya, date to about 1.76 Ma, and those at Kokiselei to 1.7–1.6 Ma.
It spread from Africa to Asia, the Middle East and Europe between 1.5 Ma and about 800,000 years ago, reaching southern India by 1.51 Ma.
Its end is poorly defined; counting the Sangoan, it lasted until as late as 130,000 years ago.

verification.title: Early Homo erectus lived at high altitudes and produced both Oldowan and Acheulean tools

facts.text: Hominins lived at Dmanisi, Georgia, from about 1.8 Ma; their fossils are the oldest human skeletal remains known outside Africa.
Fossils and tools span 1.85 to 1.77 million years, the earliest well-dated hominin fossils in Eurasia; argon dating gives 1.81 ± 0.03 Ma.
The site yielded five skulls, including Skull 5, the first complete adult hominin skull from the Early Pleistocene, plus stone tools and animal fossils.
The fossils, classed as Homo erectus georgicus, resemble early African Homo so much that all early Homo may be one species.
One toothless elderly skull has been read as early evidence of care for the old or disabled.

facts.text: The Olduvai subchron, a spell of normal magnetic polarity within the reversed Matuyama chron, lasted from about 1.95 to 1.77 Ma.
The Calabrian Age begins at 1.8 Ma, just above the top of the Olduvai chronozone and the extinction of the nannofossil Discoaster brouweri.
Its reference section is at Vrica, near Crotone in Calabria, southern Italy.
Before 2009 this level, then dated 1.806 Ma, was the base of the Pleistocene.

conflicts.note: recalculated start of the Calabrian (older chart)

title: Wolf event: Canis spreads across Eurasia

facts.text: Around 1.8 Ma Canis evolution exploded across Eurasia in what is called the wolf event.
The large wolf C. falconeri appeared abruptly in Europe, and C. borjgali lived at Dmanisi 1.8–1.75 Ma.
Coyote and wolf lineages split about 1.5 Ma; the first coyotes appear about 1.0 Ma and the first wolves about 810,000 years ago.

title: Earliest possible use of fire
article: Control of fire by early humans

facts.text: Charred bones deep in Wonderwerk Cave, South Africa, beyond the reach of wildfires, show human use of fire about 1.79 million years ago.
Other early claims include blackened bones at Yuanmou, China, about 1.7 Ma, and reddened, heated sediment at Koobi Fora, Kenya, about 1.5 Ma.
Some studies read Homo erectus' smaller molars as a sign of cooking by about 1.8 Ma; in Africa people may have scavenged fire from frequent wildfires by 1.6 Ma.

facts.text: The earliest Diprotodon fossils, indirectly dated, come from the Nelson Bay Formation in New South Wales and are 1.77 million to 780,000 years old.
Diprotodon was the largest marsupial that ever lived and the largest herbivore in Australia.
Most specimens are younger than 110,000 years; the oldest directly dated fossils, from Floraville, are about 340,000 years old.

title: Homo erectus reaches China and Java

facts.text: Homo erectus was at Yuanmou in southern China by 1.7 Ma and at Sangiran on Java by 1.66 Ma.
A Lantian cranium dates to 1.63 Ma, and stone tools in northern China's Nihewan basin to 1.7–1.6 Ma.
Yunxian Man in China is dated to 1.77 Ma; Java's Mojokerto child, once put at 1.81 Ma, is now dated to at most 1.49 Ma.
By 1.3 Ma Oldowan tools had reached as far north as the 40th parallel at Xiaochangliang.
By 1 Ma Homo erectus had spread across Eurasia, mostly south of the 50th parallel.

facts.text: The australopithecines, which had arisen in East Africa around 4 Ma, died out about 1.7 Ma.
South Africa may have been their last refuge until about 2 Ma, amid growing climatic volatility and competition from Homo and Paranthropus.
Around 2.07 Ma, just before Paranthropus robustus and Homo erectus arrived, Australopithecus africanus died out in South Africa's Cradle of Humankind.

conflicts.note: A. africanus extinct in the Cradle of Humankind

title: Bandelier Tuff eruptions form Valles Caldera

facts.text: In New Mexico's Jemez Mountains, the Toledo eruption 1.61 Ma laid down the Otowi member of the Bandelier Tuff.
It produced 216–550 km³ of dense rock; the larger estimate puts it at the low end of supereruptions (VEI 8).
A second great eruption about 1.25 Ma laid down the Tshirege member and formed the Valles Caldera, one of the best-studied resurgent calderas.

conflicts.note: Valles Caldera page (2022 cite): Tshirege member

title: Turkana Boy, a young Homo erectus

facts.text: Turkana Boy (KNM-WT 15000), a Homo erectus youth who lived 1.6–1.5 Ma near Lake Turkana, Kenya, is the most complete H. erectus skeleton ever found.
Some authorities assign it to Homo ergaster.
Its spinal column could not have supported the well-developed breathing muscles needed for speech.
The oldest Pleistocene Missoula floods swept through the Channeled Scablands sometime before 1.5 million years ago.
The age rests on interglacial calcretes between flood deposits, magnetostratigraphy and luminescence dating.
Mammoths migrated into North America around 1.5 Ma, while gomphotheres spread into South America in the Great American Interchange.
Their spread south of Alaska, about 1.4 Ma, is often used to end the Blancan and start the Irvingtonian land-mammal age.
Mammoths had left Africa in the late Pliocene, about 3.6–3.2 Ma.
The steppe mammoth arose in East Asia around 1.7 Ma and crossed the Bering Land Bridge 1.5–1.3 Ma, giving rise to the Columbian mammoth.
DNA from a 1.1–1.65-million-year-old Siberian tooth reveals the Krestovka lineage, probably the first mammoths to colonise the Americas.

Mammoth page: steppe mammoth crosses Beringia

title: Ubeidiya: Homo erectus in the Levant

facts.text: Ubeidiya, just south of the Sea of Galilee in the Jordan Rift Valley, preserves one of the earliest migrations of Homo erectus out of Africa, about 1.5 Ma.
Its layers hold Oldowan and early Acheulean tools, the Acheulean ones about 1.4 million years old.
A hominin vertebra from the site seems to belong to a different species than the Dmanisi hominins.

facts.text: Yellowstone's second cycle peaked about 1.3 Ma in the Mesa Falls Tuff eruption, over 280 km³, forming Henry's Fork Caldera inside the Island Park Caldera.
High-precision argon dating puts the eruption at 1.3001 ± 0.0006 Ma.

title: Hominins reach the island of Flores

facts.text: The ancestors of Homo floresiensis probably reached Flores between about 1.27 and 1 Ma; no stone tools there are older than 1.27 Ma.
The oldest stone tools on Flores are about 1 million years old.
Getting there meant crossing open sea; Homo erectus may have built rafts by about 840,000–800,000 years ago.

facts.text: Between about 1.25 and 0.7 Ma, glacial cycles lengthened from about 41,000 years to asymmetric 100,000-year cycles, making climate swings more extreme.
Afterwards, long cold spells built thick, higher and less slippery ice sheets, which ended in rapid jumps to warm interglacials.
Around 850,000 ± 50,000 years ago, orbital eccentricity replaced axial tilt as the main pacemaker of the ice ages.
Models reproduce the shift with falling atmospheric CO2 and glaciers gradually scraping regolith off the northern continents.
The severe glacial MIS 22 brought widespread aridity to Africa and may have caused a bottleneck in human ancestors about 1 Ma.
The Gregory Rift, the eastern branch of the East African Rift, began spreading about 1.2 Ma and still opens about 3 mm a year.
Faulting around 1.2 Ma followed large shield-volcano eruptions near the craton's edge between 5 and 1 Ma.
The last members of Paranthropus, the robust hominins, died out about 1.2 Ma.
One chronology has Australopithecus and Paranthropus making stone tools until their extinction, no later than 1.1 Ma.
The youngest Paranthropus boisei fossil, OH 80 from Olduvai Gorge, is about 1.34 million years old, though the species may have lasted to 1 Ma.

conflicts.note: youngest P. boisei record (OH 80); may have persisted to 1 Ma
P. boisei lead: end of its range

facts.text: About 1.2 Ma the earliest known of at least four caldera-forming eruptions struck Toba on Sumatra, the volcano of the later Youngest Toba eruption.
Homo antecessor, 'pioneer man', is recorded at Spain's Sierra de Atapuerca from 1.2 to 0.8 Ma, among the first people to settle Western Europe.
Cut-marked bones at Fuente Nueva-3, about 1.2 Ma, show archaic humans, probably H. antecessor, butchering the horse Equus altidens.
Once proposed as the last common ancestor of modern humans and Neanderthals, it is now seen as a side branch splitting just before them.

conflicts.note: Timeline of Earth: Homo antecessor evolves

facts.text: An asteroid blasted a 10.5 km crater in Ghana about 1.07 Ma; Lake Bosumtwi, about 8 km across, now fills it.
Tektites from the impact lie in neighbouring Ivory Coast, and related microtektites in deep-sea sediments west of Africa.
Before the impact the area was a lush rainforest.
About 1 Ma the Mangakino caldera produced the VEI 8 Kidnappers eruption, about 1,200 km³ of ignimbrite and 2,760 km³ in total.
Its ignimbrite, covering over 45,000 km², is the most widespread on Earth.
Eruptions about 1.25 and 1.0 Ma spread ignimbrite sheets across the North Island from Auckland to Napier.

verification.title: Generation and Rejuvenation of a Supervolcanic Magmatic System: a Case Study from Mangakino Volcanic Centre, New Zealand

title: Kilimanjaro's Kibo and Mawenzi cones begin erupting

facts.text: Kibo and Mawenzi, two of Kilimanjaro's three volcanic cones, began erupting about 1 million years ago; the older Shira centre had been active since 2.4 million years ago.
Kibo, the largest cone, built up in lava phases dated from about 482,000 to 170,000 years ago; its last activity, 200,000–150,000 years ago, formed the summit crater.
Kilimanjaro, at 5,895 m the highest peak in Africa, is a dormant stratovolcano; Kibo still has gas-emitting fumaroles in its crater.
The Pannonian Sea, a shallow landlocked sea in Central Europe since about 10 Ma, lasted until about 1 Ma.
By then 3–4 km of sediment had filled the Pannonian Basin.
Earth's field briefly returned to normal polarity within the reversed Matuyama chron, usually dated from 990,000 to 950,000 years ago.
Some studies start it at 1.07 Ma instead; the causes of such short reversals are still disputed.
A proposed link to the Bosumtwi impact has been called highly speculative and refuted.
Hominin footprints pressed into sediment at Happisburgh, Norfolk, between about 950,000 and 850,000 years ago are the oldest known outside Africa.
They are the first evidence of early humans this far north, alongside flint tools from the same deposits.
The makers may have been Homo antecessor; the beds lie between the Jaramillo and Brunhes–Matuyama reversals.

title: Palaeoloxodon elephants spread out of Africa

facts.text: At the end of the Early Pleistocene, about 800,000 years ago, the elephant genus Palaeoloxodon spread out of Africa and across Eurasia.
About 790,000 years ago a large impact scattered tektites across the enormous Australasian strewnfield.
Its crater has not been found; one about 100 km wide in Indochina, perhaps under Tonlé Sap in Cambodia, has been suggested.
Artifacts found with its tektites tie a Homo erectus population to the impact and its aftermath.
A link to the Brunhes–Matuyama reversal is highly speculative; the two probably only happened around the same time.

title: Fire and cooking at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov

facts.text: Around 780,000 years ago, hominins at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in northern Israel left traces of fire and the oldest likely evidence of cooking, mainly heated fish teeth.
It is the oldest established continuous fire site outside Africa; H. erectus or H. ergaster is claimed to have controlled fire there 790,000–690,000 years ago.
Its inhabitants gathered and ate 55 kinds of fruits, vegetables, seeds, nuts and tubers.
